```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
tutorial_options(exercise.timelimit = 30)
```

## Why this tutorial

If you must report **one number** for an uncertain quantity, which one? It depends on how you are penalised for
being wrong. This warmup makes that precise and also shows why the posterior mode (MAP) needs care.

About 40 minutes.

## 1. Choosing a number by minimising expected loss

Take draws from a skewed belief, Beta(2, 12). For any guess `g`, we can compute the *average loss* over the
draws. Try three loss functions: squared error, absolute error and 0-1 loss (counts as correct only if within
0.01 of the truth).

```{r loss, exercise=TRUE, exercise.lines=18}
set.seed(1)
draws <- rbeta(2e4, 2, 12)
guess <- seq(0.01, 0.4, by = 0.005)

sq  <- sapply(guess, function(g) mean((draws - g)^2))
ae  <- sapply(guess, function(g) mean(abs(draws - g)))
zo  <- sapply(guess, function(g) mean(abs(draws - g) > 0.01))

best <- c(squared = guess[which.min(sq)],
          absolute = guess[which.min(ae)],
          zero_one = guess[which.min(zo)])
best
c(mean = 2 / 14, median = qbeta(0.5, 2, 12), mode = 1 / 12)
```

The three minimisers land (up to grid resolution and simulation noise) on the **mean**, the **median** and
the **mode**.

```{r quiz-loss}
quiz(
  question("Squared-error loss is minimised by the posterior:",
    answer("mean", correct = TRUE),
    answer("median"),
    answer("mode"),
    allow_retry = TRUE),
  question("Absolute-error loss is minimised by the posterior:",
    answer("median", correct = TRUE),
    answer("mean"),
    answer("mode"),
    allow_retry = TRUE),
  question("An all-or-nothing loss (right only if you hit the value) is minimised by the posterior:",
    answer("mode (the MAP)", correct = TRUE),
    answer("mean"),
    answer("median"),
    allow_retry = TRUE)
)
```

## 2. They differ when the density is skewed

For a symmetric density they agree. For Beta(2, 12), mean 0.143, median 0.126 and mode 0.083 are visibly
different. Edit the code to see how they converge as the sample size `a + b` grows with the same mean.

```{r converge, exercise=TRUE, exercise.lines=12}
m <- 1 / 7                    # keep the mean fixed
n <- c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500)
a <- m * n; b <- (1 - m) * n
data.frame(n,
           mean   = a / (a + b),
           median = qbeta(0.5, a, b),
           mode   = ifelse(a > 1 & b > 1, (a - 1) / (a + b - 2), NA))
```

(The mode formula only applies when `a > 1` and `b > 1`. Warmup A covered the other cases.)

## 3. The MAP is not invariant to reparameterisation

Posterior *mean* of $\theta$ and posterior *median* of $\theta$ behave sensibly if we change variables (the median
of $\log\theta$ is the log of the median of $\theta$). The **mode does not**. Gamma(2, 1) has mode 1, mean 2,
median 1.678. What is the mode of $\log X$?

```{r mode-log, exercise=TRUE, exercise.lines=12}
set.seed(1)
x <- rgamma(1e6, 2, 1)
d_x <- density(x)
d_l <- density(log(x))
c(mode_of_x         = d_x$x[which.max(d_x$y)],
  log_of_mode_of_x  = log(d_x$x[which.max(d_x$y)]),
  mode_of_log_x     = d_l$x[which.max(d_l$y)],
  log_of_median_x   = log(median(x)),
  median_of_log_x   = median(log(x)))
```

The mode of $\log X$ (about 0.69, which is $\log 2$) is **not** the log of the mode of $X$ (which is 0).

```{r quiz-invariance}
quiz(
  question("You report a MAP of the PPV. A colleague reports a MAP of the log-odds of the PPV. These two MAPs:",
    answer("generally correspond to different PPV values.", correct = TRUE,
           message = "The density changes shape under the transformation (a Jacobian factor)."),
    answer("always correspond to the same PPV value.", message = "That is true for the median, not for the mode."),
    answer("are the same only when the prior is flat.", message = "A flat prior on one scale is not flat on the other."),
    allow_retry = TRUE)
)
```

## 4. A probability statement: P(PPV > threshold)

Sometimes the number to report is not a center but a **probability**: "how sure are we that the PPV exceeds
0.5?" With draws it is just the fraction of draws above the threshold. (Team 4's `prob_exceeds`.)

```{r exceed, exercise=TRUE, exercise.lines=10}
set.seed(1)
ppv_fn <- function(se, sp, prev) {
  tp <- se * prev; fp <- (1 - sp) * (1 - prev); tp / (tp + fp)
}
ppv <- ppv_fn(rbeta(1e5, 18, 2), rbeta(1e5, 95, 5), 0.08)
mean(ppv > 0.5)
mean(ppv >= 0.8)
```

Here P(PPV > 0.5) is large (about 0.9) and P(PPV >= 0.8) is small (a few percent).

```{r quiz-exceed}
quiz(
  question("Why does `mean(ppv > 0.5)` estimate a probability?",
    answer("`ppv > 0.5` is TRUE/FALSE for each draw, and the mean of TRUE/FALSE is the fraction TRUE.", correct = TRUE),
    answer("`mean()` always returns a probability.", message = "It returns an average, which here happens to be a fraction."),
    answer("Because the draws are between 0 and 1.", message = "That is irrelevant to the comparison."),
    allow_retry = TRUE)
)
```

### Where this leads

Teams 1 and 4 write the mean, median and mode functions and `prob_exceeds`. The app puts mean, median and MAP
on the same plot so you can *see* these differences.
